voice: Plain, calm, direct. Written for an owner reading on a phone between calls.
Formal and warm. Write as a professional firm addressing a managing director. Never casual, never coach-style hype.
Name the pain first, then the other way. Never open on our features.
Say the owner's own words: chase, follow-up, slipped. Not workflow orchestration, not digital transformation.
Respectful of how hard the owner already works. Never scold, never make them feel behind.
Numbers in digits. Rupee amounts written Rs 20,000, never the rupee glyph.
Sentence case. Eyebrows in small capitals. No ALL CAPS, no exclamation marks, no emoji.
Every piece is written in the order Problem, Impact, Solution.
English operational nouns: follow-up, status, pending, dispatch, payment, reminder.
One Hindi tag only inside a quoted owner line (Task hua?, ho gaya?). Never whole Hindi sentences, never in our own voice.
Say my family's firm or my family's company openly. Name Voltas, Panasonic, GPC and Georgia Tech only as places the founder worked or studied.
The founder is a designer who builds systems, never a systems expert or an automation expert. The word that carries the story is designed.
The caption carries all three beats: the owner's moment, what it costs, and the tool we built and run. A caption that stops at the problem is half a piece.
Hashtags in lower case, five at most on Instagram, three at most on the last line of a LinkedIn post, never in the body.

Holiday, mourning and compliance-day rules override the calendar every time.
The piece is in the order Problem, Impact, Solution, and the middle beat is an impact, not a second problem.
The hook is eight words or fewer.
No emoji, no exclamation marks, no ALL CAPS.
Instagram: hashtags at the end only, within the limit. LinkedIn: none in the body, three at the bottom at most.
No promised saving, hours or rupee figure that is not clearly marked as an example. No crore or x-times figure.
No client, lender or staff name, and no company name outside the allowed list.
The solution line names a tool from the Solutions list or says plainly what it does; never system alone.

At most one Hindi tag, and only inside a quoted owner line.
The register is formal and warm; nothing casual, nothing coach-style.
Every video ends on the same end card: logo, tagline. Captions in white on a dark bar.
Scheduled posts are queued no more than 48 hours ahead and the scheduler is checked each morning.
The piece names the tool we built (the reminder desk, the owner's screen, My Day, the weekly score, the question tray) where it speaks of a system, a screen or a list.
A LinkedIn post ends with one question; a Status rule marks its phrase in stars; Instagram hashtags are lower case and five at most.
No square-bracket placeholder remains in any field.

If you are the owner of a business with a few dozen people, you probably spend your day asking whether things are done. Work goes out when you remember it, and you find out what slipped when a client calls. This is not new software. We build the system that does that chasing for you, on your own Google Sheet, so your data stays yours. It hands the work to the right person, follows it up and records it. Every Monday the work goes out. Every Friday you get the score, and you hold one sit-down a week for what only you can decide. We set it up, train your team and keep it running. We run the system; your team still does the work. We start with one process, so you see it working before you add the next. It is the same system that runs my family's firm in Indore every day.

frame: Venture Drafters builds the tools that run a business, on the owner's own Google account, and runs them with the owner every week. The owner's problem is a design problem: work has no home, no visible state and no feedback loop. We run the system; the team still does the work. Never say the business runs by itself.
